title: Shilou's Shortcomings
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer encourages listeners to let go of unrealistic expectations and blame, instead embracing the imperfections of themselves and the world around them. By acknowledging both their own flaws and the difficulties faced by others, we can cultivate hope for long-term change and trust in the inherent goodness of human nature. This approach allows us to see ourselves and others as they truly are, rather than trying to fit into narrow or idealized categories, and to find meaning and purpose in our ongoing efforts to grow and learn.

sentences.text: *An unsurpassed, penetrating and perfect dharma is rarely met with even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
Morning everybody.
Nice to see you all, and I can see many of you.
Very sweet.
Today I have another story for you from Dogen's 300 stories.
This is story number 50: Shiloh's Shortcomings.
*Shiloh was asked by a monastic, "I don't know the original nature yet.
Master, please show me by skillful means."
And Shiloh said, "I don't have earlobes,"* meaning I can't hear you.
What did you say?
I'm not hearing you.
*And the monastic said, "I know I have shortcomings."
And Shiloh said, "Well, this old monastic has faults too."
And the monastic said, "What are your faults?"
And Shiloh said, "My faults lie in your shortcomings."
The monastic bowed, and Shiloh hit him.*
What a great story, right?
It reminds me of what I hear people so often say.
I feel so helpless.
I feel so bad.
There's so much wrong with me, or there's so much wrong in the world.
And I feel complicit.
I feel so privileged.
I try to do what I can, but it's never enough, or I'm never enough, or I'm such a mess, or maybe I have no idea what to do.
Can you please help me?
What should I do?
Well, the world has always been a rough place.
I don't think you can find a moment in history where there was fairness and justice for all.
So where did we ever get the idea that it ought to be different now?
We should be realistic and have a little historical perspective.
This is the world.
This is us.
This is what we do.
This is what we have always done.
This is maybe what we will always do.
This is the world.
And yet, and yet, we have another idea, don't we?
And it's so beautiful that we have another idea.
Despite this, we have a different idea.
We have the idea that the world could be a better place, even a good place.
We have the idea, despite all the odds, that there could be somehow justice and peace in this world.
What an amazing idea!
Where did we ever get such a crazy idea?
Is it just like some big delusion?
Maybe.
Maybe it's a big delusion.
But I think it's our delusion, and we come by it quite honestly.

Just as we know that we human beings are always going to be subject to greed, hate, and delusion, that's in us, that's actually built into what we are as an organism, that's built into the way our mind and bodies work, so also it is built into us to have the imagination to project ideas of goodness onto a longed-for future.
If we have to admit, sadly, that injustice and violence is a part of who we are, then we also admit that goodness and the wish for peace and love is also who we are.
Both these things are absolutely true of us.

It's not that we find ourselves involved in this primordial struggle of good versus evil, or worse than that: we, the good guys, the Buddhists, or the lefties, or the Democrats, or whoever we think we are, doing battle with them, the bad guys.
No.
Actually, the story is much more nuanced than that.
As the Shiloh and the monastic dialogue shows us, we are the good guys and the bad guys.
Without our greed, hate, and delusion, there is no vision of goodness.
Without the vision of goodness, there is no greed, hate, and delusion.
The bad guys are right to be the way they are, to express on behalf of all of us who we are in our fullness.
One of the most wonderful of all of Thich Nhat Hanh's very famous teachings is that Buddha needs Mara, and Mara needs Buddha.
Human life is a journey, it's a story with a beginning and an end that keeps on repeating.
Our practice is to affirm the goodness, and understand the evil, and embrace it with love.
Because that's how the story goes forward into a new chapter.
As bodhisattvas, we have a long, long view.
You know the Mahayana Sutras that talk about many, many, many lifetimes of practice throughout world systems for a bodhisattva.
Long view.
Right now, people are still in the streets speaking out against injustice.
And it's been a very inspiring and hopeful moment, even in the midst of this pandemic.
Probably because of this pandemic that has opened our hearts so much, we care even more than we did before.
And I really do feel like a lot of good is going to come from this moment.
The moment for real reform is here.
And I really hope that's true, and I know you hope that's true also.
But don't we know, too, that six months from today, this passion for the good that we're feeling as we're feeling it now is going to be a memory?
And there's going to be something else occupying our thoughts.
I think some things will really change now for the good.
Things do advance, and they will advance as a result of what's happening now.

But also probably we all understand that some really important things that absolutely need to change will not change, and that the overwhelming likelihood is that we will return to the human muddle, which is where we always end up in between the big swings this way and the big swings that way.
We're back to the ordinary human muddling through.

So let's not be too foolishly hopeful in the short run, because then we're going to really be disappointed, and our disappointment will get us depressed and make it so we won't feel motivated to do things.
We'll be discouraged.
So let's not be unrealistically hopeful in the short run, but let's be powerfully hopeful in the long run.
Let's have the absolute faith and confidence that in the long run we are going in the direction of justice and peace.
Of course it's going to take a long time.
Look how long it took to make this mess, but we're getting there.
No matter how it looks at any given point, we are getting there.
And it makes me think of many, many decades ago.
I'm sure there are a few of you here old enough to remember this moment.
I forget what year it was, but it was in the 1960s, late 1960s.

And I was in my college apartment watching the daily news, as I always did, and watching the president, Lyndon Johnson, announce with a grave face that he was stopping the bombing in Vietnam and not running for reelection.
And we leaped off of the couch, shrieking and yelling, because we won!
The war was over, the bad guy was gone, and peace and justice would finally rule over the earth.
We saw that.
It was true.
It didn't take long for us to be very disappointed.
Then we got Nixon and bombing of Cambodia and everything else.
It also makes me think of some years after that, going for the first time to Israel, where I have lots of relatives and connections.
And I was very discouraged about how things were then.
Of course, now they're ten times worse.
Who thought they could get worse?
And I remember meeting an old guy there, who had been there before the founding of the state.
He was one of the settlers in the 30s.
So he had been through a lot in Europe before he immigrated, and in Israel.
And I remember saying to him, "How could you ever get to peace from where we are now?"

And I remember him saying to me joyfully, as if he were absolutely certain this was so, and I don't know where he got this from, but I'll never forget, he said to me, "Everything is always going toward peace."
Everything is always going toward peace.
I believe it.
It's the truth.
Even though a lot of times it doesn't look like that.
Sitting in silence, touching the heart, I think we come to be like that guy.
We know that.
And it doesn't have to do with facts or sophisticated historical knowledge or analysis.
Nobody knows anything about history.
Nobody has any idea about what happens next.
It doesn't have to do with that.
It has to do with knowing what it means to have a human heart.
It has to do with being in touch with one's own heart.
The other day I was talking about Professor Ibram Kendi.
One of the most challenging and eye-opening things that he says: he talks about not racists, but racist ideas.
He says there are two kinds of racist ideas.
The first kind is the one we've always been familiar with.
It's the one that says that black people or brown people or any people other than your own people are inferior somehow.
Morally inferior, intellectually inferior, culturally inferior.
Your culture is the best, and their culture, well, it's lacking.
So their people in that culture are lacking.
So this kind of racism really was common throughout human history.
It believed in an Aristotelian worldview, which is a world of hierarchy.
Heaven above, earth below, the rulers should rule over the ruled, men should be over women, and so naturally one race should be over another.
It was just natural, the natural order of things.
Many centuries that was a common human view, but now we don't live in that world anymore.
We find that view abhorrent.
It's really hard to support that kind of a racist idea.
And probably, I hope, it's becoming more rare.
You don't find so many people who actually believe in this kind of racist idea, or at least will admit to believing in this kind of racist idea.
It's so embarrassing.
It's now considered to be an outrageous and impossible idea to hold.
That's why when we hear this talk about racism, it's so shocking.
Where are the racists?
They're all gone, we think.
But there's a second kind of racist idea that Professor Kendi talks about, and this one is more challenging.
This kind of racist idea holds that all races are equal.
Of course they are.
There is no hierarchy of races.
But the trouble is, because of oppression and deprivation in the past, some races, because they were so unfairly treated, have become wounded.
And so they're not able to perform at the level of other races.
And it's not that they're inferior in any way, but it's because of what's been done to them that they have these problems.
So that's why people of the superior racial group, who have had the advantages, must understand this and repair the damage so that the inferior race will eventually be able to become equal.
The truth is, this is a common view.
Actually, it might be the most common view still.
Although most people who, consciously or unconsciously, have that view don't consider it to be a racist view, Professor Kendi is saying it is.
Even though the intentions of people who feel that way may be quite good, they don't understand the kind of prejudice that's actually built into such a view.
And when you think about it, this is really a big challenge, right?
Because don't we all partially at least believe that?
Isn't that why, if we feel guilty and paralyzed, because we think we're in a superior position, and we've caused our brothers and sisters to be in an inferior position, isn't that what we're saying?

Doesn't our very belief in social and economic determinism, which actually we believe mostly, doesn't even our sophisticated understanding of trauma, which is caused by psychological and economic deprivation, doesn't that also tell us that this is so?
And if all of that were not so, then what?
How would we understand this?
And the reason I'm bringing this up, and I hasten to say that obviously I don't know so much about all this, I'm not speaking here as an expert on this, I'm giving you my own thoughts and questions.
And I'm bringing it up now because it is our duty, all of us, to try to understand our own understanding.
What are we thinking here?
How are we thinking?
But also I'm bringing it up today because it reminds me of something I was recently studying in the Dharma just a few weeks ago.
I was studying Dogen's teaching on causality from Shobogenzo's Ui Monki.
Just in case you're interested, it's book one, number six.
And I gave a Dharma talk about that particular section of Shobogenzo's Ui Monki in our Dharma seminar at the end of May.
And so obviously I'm not going to repeat my whole Dharma talk, but just to make it short, it's a dialogue between Dogen and Ejo about causality.
And Dogen is talking about the famous story that I'm sure many of you know about Nanquan's cat.
And he's also referencing the story of Baijiang's fox.
And these are the two most important stories in the Zen tradition about causality, about karma.
And they're very nuanced and complex.
And in the course of his comments on these stories, Dogen says something like this: cause and effect is not, as we think they are, a linear sequence.

And when you think about it, of course Dogen would say that, because we all know that one of Dogen's main points that we're constantly practicing all the time, even though we forget it constantly too, is enlightenment is not a result of the cause of practice.
We practice and then we get enlightened later on as a linear cause of our practice.
No, Dogen says that is not at all the case.
He says practice is enlightenment.
Practice and enlightenment are simultaneous.
Practice doesn't bring us to enlightenment or lead us to enlightenment.
It is enlightenment at every point.
And we're always struggling.
How could that be?
What does Dogen mean by that?
How do we live that?
But he applies this same way of understanding to causality.
And at one point in the discussion he talks to Nanquan.
As you know in the cat story, Nanquan says to the monastics who are disputing about a cat, "Say a word, a true word, or I'm going to cut the cat in two," and nobody can say anything.
And he cuts the cat in two.
And Dogen says to him, eight, nine hundred years later, Dogen says to him, "Nanquan, you think you're so smart, you know how to cut a cat in two.
How about cutting a cat into one?"
So this made me think about, today's my nostalgia day I guess, This made me think about the early 1990s, when I was teaching at our local high school.
I live at Muir Beach, which is a little community off to the side, but our local high school is in Mill Valley.
Mill Valley is a white, mostly white, well-off community, like many other communities in our county.
But there is actually a nearby African-American enclave that is not well-off.

The students from that small community have their own elementary school and their own middle school, but they go to the white town, Mill Valley, for high school, and I had them when I taught high school there.
I really wanted to understand them better, so I did an after-school writing group for them.
It took me a long time to convince them to come.
I had to really struggle to get them to come, but they came, and we had a really great writing group.
Long story.
It was really beautiful for me.
During that same time, I also offered a meditation class in the African-American Community Day Care Center for the women who took care of the children.
I would go there once a week and offer meditation and so on, and so I got to know people in the community a little bit.
Now, these were people who were understood by all the white people in the community to be members of a severely deprived group, and they were.
They were in crisis: tons of unemployment, lots of single-family households, lots of drug abuse, lots of problems.
For this reason, they were pretty much, even now, written off by the white community.
It was as if they didn't exist.
People would say, "Oh, it's a white county."
Then you'd say, "But what about Marin City?"
That's the name of the community.
And they'd say, "Oh, yeah, right, Marin City," as if it wasn't even there.
It was really a forgotten place because of these poor, unfortunate people who lived in it, about whom really nothing could be done, that anybody could think of.
What could we do?
But when I went into the community, I had a totally different experience.
Yeah, it's true there were social problems.
It's true there was plenty of suffering in the community.
But there was a liveliness.
There was a depth.
There was a joy.
There was a love.
There was a texture of culture that really amazed me.
When people would ask me, I used to say, "You know, in Marin City, every other person has a drug problem, and every other person is a genius or a saint."
No, I was no doubt exaggerating, as I often do.
But really, that's what it felt like.
I met so many great people.
They amazed me.
Maybe they weren't so amazing, but to me they really seemed amazing.
In other words, like everybody else, when I didn't really know the community, naturally I had an impression about it from what I read in the papers and statistics and numbers and blah, blah, blah.
Given who I was and what kind of information I consumed and what my experience was, naturally I had that point of view, and I believed it was true.

I didn't even realize that I was feeling sorry for these poor, beleaguered people in Marin City, as if they were deprived and I was not, as if their lives were lesser than mine, lesser than what they could have been or should have been because they did not have the advantages that I had.
And this is more or less, isn't it, the way white Americans think.
The most liberal, the most caring white Americans look at it that way, the way I was looking at it, and probably mostly look at it still, even though I know better, because this is the message I get.
I think also, as Professor Kendi, in talking about himself, says, middle-class, educated Black Americans can also feel that way about the community.

But when you actually go into the community, as I know perhaps one or two of you have in our session, and you get to know people, no matter who they are or what you think about them from the outside, you realize that their lives are not what you thought they were.
How could they be, when you think about it?
How could we ever possibly, in our minds, from the newspaper, understand what people are somewhere else, even though we're mesmerized by all this and we think we know?
Of course, we're only going to see our own conditioning, not people.
And the reality is that human beings are really genius.
When you get to know them, talk to somebody for a while, listen to them, whatever deprivation or suffering they have experienced, it has not diminished them.
Of course it hasn't diminished them, just as our suffering, when we have suffered, has not diminished us.
When you think about it, it's so obvious.
Buddha nature shines through everyone, maybe even stronger when you've been through a lot.
Suffering doesn't deform people, it makes them more beautiful.
And you don't need to feel badly or guilty or feel somehow you need to raise up these people.
In fact, as it turned out, I was learning a lot more from them than they were learning from me.
I was receiving a lot more than I was giving.
I didn't even think I was giving anyway.
I knew that I was there for myself.
And it's good that I didn't think I was giving anything, because I wasn't.
They didn't need me.
I was the one who was being helped.

So when Professor Kendi says the anti-racist view is to see that all races are equal, really equal, despite the oppression of the past, he's pointing to something really important and essential for us to understand.
Really, it's a Dharma teaching.
Now, he's not saying that everybody is perfect and everybody's a genius and all this.
That's a romantic view.
No doubt, there are problems.
People have problems.
He says you can find lazy people and bad people, confused people, people with drug problems, people with mental health problems, and so on.
But he says, if I'm understanding him and reading him correctly, that these problems are distributed evenly throughout the racial groups.
We can't say this racial group has those problems and this racial group doesn't.
And it was true in my experience teaching in the high school.
There were proportionally as many messed up white kids from the affluent suburb as there were messed up black kids.
And if it was true, and I'm not even sure that it was true, that proportionally the black kids didn't do as well in school, it wasn't because they were deprived or not as smart.
It was because the school was a white institution, and its values and ways of speaking and understanding were white.
Maybe the black students were not as good at being white as the white students were.
But it's debatable whether it's worthwhile to be that good at being white, although, for sure, our society gives you a lot of credit for that.
It might not be something worth aspiring to.
So I was lucky to have that short time with those black students, and I really loved them a lot.
I don't know if they even noticed that I was there, to tell you the truth, but I really got a lot from them.
Now the thing is, of course it goes without saying that we should be of service where there are problems.
And there are problems, of course there are problems, and we should be of service.
But here's the thing: the idea that the people we are trying to serve have somehow been degraded or diminished and so are in need of our help, that's patronizing.
And it's just not true.
Every person is an awesome Buddha.
This is the cornerstone of our tradition in Mahayana Buddhism.
This is what Dogen is constantly saying.
We don't have to strive to become enlightened Buddhas.
We already are.
Practice helps us to remember this and appreciate it, but even if we don't practice, we're that anyway by virtue of our being living, sacred human beings.
Look at any person and see that person.
Help that person, of course, in whatever way you are able to.
It's your obligation as a human being.
But don't think that that person is in need of help that you are not also in need of, and that you can provide.
Help because it's the right thing to do.
Help because it's the loving thing to do.
Help because you are human and this is what humans do, and because when you help, you'll feel your humanity more deeply and you'll become a happier and better person.
And we read in the beginning of the Diamond Sutra about the practice of generosity, of giving: there is no giver, no gift, no recipient of a gift, and no giving.
There is only the love that is the true foundation of our lives.
And when we miss that, we suffer.
When we feel it, we have joy, even in the midst of suffering.
So in [unclear: "Chobo Genzo's Ui Monki"], Dogen is saying, quite astonishingly, that cause and effect are not linear, just like awakening and practice.
They're simultaneous.
What could that mean?
This is a deep thought about morality and causality, and I'm not sure that I really know what it means.
But maybe it means that the effects of moral action are immediate.
It means that the idea that we have, that the oppressors win and the oppressed lose, is a superficial idea.
Bodhisattvas have a loving vision of [unclear: "Buddha-I"] that pierces the surface of things and sees that oppressors don't win and the oppressed don't lose.
My ostensible advantage over someone else does not make me advantaged.
In fact, it diminishes me.
It diminishes my love and my humanity.

The idea that we ought to overcome racism and economic injustice for the benefit of marginalized racial groups and the poor, so that they can be more like us, doesn't go deeply enough into the heart of the matter.
We have to do these things for ourselves, for all of us, because it's the right thing to do and because it's necessary for us all to realize ourselves and to perfect our love.
We take care of others, not for others whom we think need it, but for ourselves.
And we take care of ourselves for others.
This is what we were saying yesterday.
It's not upside down and crazy, but for bodhisattvas looking at the world, it's the world that's upside down and crazy, and boy is it ever.
So Yangshan puts on his socks for others when it's cold.
Shiloh was asked by a monastic, "I don't know the original nature yet.
Master, please show me by skillful means."
And Shiloh said, "I don't have earlobes."
And the monastic said, "I know I have shortcomings."
Shiloh said, "What are your faults?"
Or rather, the monastic said, "What are your faults?"
And Shiloh said, "My faults lie in your shortcomings."
The monastic bowed and Shiloh hit him.

Of course Shiloh can't hear the monastic when the monastic is asking that he, Shiloh, should apply skillful means and enlighten the monastic, as if Shiloh has something that the monastic lacks, and the monastic is saying, "Please give me that thing that I lack."
Of course Shiloh can't hear that.
No one has anything somebody else needs.
To think this is so is to fall into the trap of attachment aversion, the trap of thinking you have something that does not exist.
You don't have it to begin with.
The monastic says, "Well, I'm asking because I have shortcomings, and I'm hoping you can help me eliminate them."
Well, I have shortcomings too.
"What are your shortcomings?"
My shortcomings are your shortcomings.
We have shortcomings, right.
We have shortcomings together.
This is us.
This is the world we have made.
Take a look at all of it, not just the parts you like.
Take a look at the shortcomings of the people you are mad at, the people who you think are responsible for ruining this world.
They are your shortcomings too.
And of course we fight the fight.
We do what needs to be done.
We express our strong opposition to what we know is wrong.
But we don't forget who we are.
The monastic bowed.
Apparently the monastic deeply heard what Shiloh was saying.
And then Shiloh hit her, or him, because we never understand deeply enough.
We don't.
We spur each other on.
We help each other in our endless search for truth and goodness.
And we're wrong a lot of the time.
I'm not sure, but I think that a chat popped up while I was talking here.
I think someone, I'll have to look at it later.
I think someone in the session was already correcting me for stuff that I said already that's wrong.
I think I'll look in the chat and find out.
I have no doubt that that will happen.
Dharma teachers don't like to talk about this stuff because they're going to be wrong and then people will yell at them for it.
I don't blame them.
I don't want to talk about it either.
I know I'm safe with you.
Besides, you're thousands of miles away.
You can't hurt me anyway.
So the point is, we don't get it.
I don't get it.
We're not going to get it.
We're going to keep trying to get it.
Maybe we got it more today than yesterday.
Or not.
Or not.
Maybe we're going backwards.
But we're going to try.
We're going to try to keep practicing and keep trying to understand.
We're never satisfied.
We're satisfied with every moment of this beautiful life, and we're never satisfied.
Our big effort to save all beings, end all delusions, enter all dharma gates, and become through and through nothing other than the Buddha way, as we're going to say in a minute, never ends.
Never ends.
So I'll close with [unclear: "Dido's"] short poem on this story.
*Where can you put this gigantic body?
There's no place to put it.
Ultimately, how is it?
When clouds gather on the mountain, thunder fills the sky.*
So thank you all very much for helping me explore these important things that we're all thinking about now.
I think it's really our job to try to understand how we can see this through a lens of dharma, and whether or not that helps for us to sustain us, and for what we can offer to others.
